None of the political story is told through action, it relies almost solely on dialogue, though there is a recurring scene with the only action, and it is a stroke of genius that allows the viewer to see a full panorama of the tense political struggle that the struggle for independence gave birth to. This film is real. It is honest inits portrayal of those in power, the corrupt and the honest. It is eye-opening in its politics. And it is moving in the passions and emotions that its characters bring to it. Whether you are interested in politics, history, history, or simply like good stories, this film is for you.

I saw an episode of Masterpiece Theatre on Netflix, and decided to look it up. I was greeted with a comment from another user, who believed that the episode was short for a 60-minute show, boring, and underwhelming. I would feel morally remiss if I didn't correct this person. Now, I am a huge fan of Masterpiece Theatre, but sometimes the stories can be hard to follow on television; for example, "He Knew He Was Right" was a bit slow. This particular episode, however, is probably the best I've seen so far. The entire cast does an excellent job, and it touched my heart more than any other piece I've seen recently. The character Mr. Evans is of particular interest, and through the images of, for example, an untouched wedding cake and a broken engagement ring, my opinion of him went from bad to truly good. I think his ultimate redemption, and the story of how everyone around him made him a much better man, is what brought out the bittersweet in this story for me. The end was gratifying in every sense as well; that everyone did not get what they deserved, and overall everything worked out. I absolutely recommend this to everyone.

Crackerjack is a simple but feelgood movie where the good guys are very good and the bad guys are very bad and the central character is tempted by both sides. The combination of the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the central setting being the local lawn bowls clubs drew an unusually broad crowd ranging from large numbers of teenagers to large numbers of senior citizens - and all laughed at the comedy. As would be expected of a movie with Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy there was quite a bit of swearing, but it was not overdone and the audience I sat with certainly enjoyed it! Mick Malloy did a good job as the lazy bloke who joined the bowls club (three times) simply to get parking spaces (one for himself and two for leasing to others at a premium) but who has everything fall down on him when he is required to play or lose his membership. Judith Lucy does a fine job as his local journalist/love-interest and there are fabulous performances from Bill Hunter, Frank Wilson, Monica Maughan, Lois Ramsey and many others. John Clarke's dour role as the bad guy is not one of his funniest but he gives a solid performance. The not so subtle swipes at pokies provide a bit of a serious note to this otherwise light comedy. I'm sure that those who enjoyed The Castle and The Dish would also enjoy this movie.

Steered text
Crackerjack is a classic example of a comedy where the good guys are very good and the bad guys are very bad and the central character is tempted by both sides. The combination of the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the story setting being in a lawn bowls club drew an entire audience - ranging from a group of teenagers to a group of senior citizens - and everyone laughed at the comedy. As would be expected in a movie with Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy there was quite a bit of swearing, but it was not gratuitous and the audience just sat there and enjoyed it. Mick Malloy does a great job as a lazy bloke who joined the bowls club (and others) simply for the parking spaces (one for himself and two for the two others at the club) but then has to fall down his hole when he is required to play or lose his job. Judith Lucy does a great job as his female journalist/love interest and there are great performances from Bill Hunter, Frank Wilson, Bill Pemberton, Peter Ramsey and many others. John Clarke's dour performance as the bad guy is not one of the funniest but he gives a solid performance and there is a not so subtle mention of suicide which adds a bit of a dark note to this otherwise light-hearted comedy. I think that those who enjoyed The Office and The Island would also enjoy this movie

The 60's series 'Department S' was a British thriller show about an elite team of Scotland Yard detectives, based in Geneva, created to solve baffling crimes the police could not handle. If a plane landed at Heathrow with no-one inside, if a man was found dead a beach in a ski-suit, if the driver of a Rolls Royce was found to be... a skeleton or if a train ran into a tube station and failed to contain its commuters, you would call 'Department S' to sort it out. The show was led by 'Jason King', a former Scotland Yard detective and crime novelist whose brilliant mind helped crack many of these bizarre cases. King was the public's favourite and was even awarded medals on the show. He was ably assisted by American detective 'Frank Sullivan' ( Peter Cushing ) and the delectable 'Daphne Hurst' ( Dianaelope Atkins ). Unusually for a 60's show, there was also a doctor in the team - 'Inspector Curtis Trotter' ( Dennis O'Sullivan )! The show had a lot of feel to 'The Avengers', which is hardly surprising. It shared many of the same writers and directors! The colourful titles were designed by Chambers and Partners and are well worth tuning in for alone. As was the case with many B.R.T.V. shows, the music was composed by Ron Grain, and and the theme for 'Department S' has to rank as one of the best TV themes of all time. Predictably, the show was a little sexist and dated at times but don't let these minor flaws deter you from tuning in. Imagine a hybrid between 'Jonathan Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' movies and you'll have 'Department S'! Fun Fact: The episode entitled 'A War Of Nerves' features a young Sir Anthony Hopkins in a minor role!

The station wants to air a story a reporter has written about a famous murder case from 20 years ago. So they hire the local preacher (James Stewart) to track down the murderess, who was acquitted and has been living quietly under a fake name. This one comes in under five stars but is a pale copy of the original which had some great performances from Edward G. Robinson, Aline MacMahon, Walter Abel, and Boris Karloff. But it's still worth watching Boagrt.

Another nice entry in the Crime Doctor series [#4/10], with atmospheric almost noirish black and white photography and some splendid Spanish American backdrops and sets. And a more off-the-wall storyline too! A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a locked room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim it murder, and so we are presented with a quite weird set of people to mull over, for one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the 3rd wife and rich widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister vampires, the intense young man, the eccentric cabinet maker Lloyd Corrigan on loan from Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds-on Jerome Cowan? Police Inspector Emory Parnell had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as Ordway was as unflappable as ever in working it all out. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: On breaking into the murder room Ordway says "Right through the centre of the forehead" and Cowan replies "He didn't miss this time". Favorite bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling through club sandwiches and beer at the nightclub to make amends for their interrupted dinner party; The scene where the Braga's place of repose is seemingly rumbled. The plot does seem to meander a bit at times and the way it was all explained off was perhaps more worthy of Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural wouldn't do either! Well worth a watch if you already like the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

A nice entry in the Doctor Doctor series [1949], with atmospheric film noirish black and white photography, some nice Spanish-style architecture in the sets, and a solid performance from Robert Ordway. A man who looks like the insane murderer from the previous two episodes is found dead in a locked room after a lavish dinner party. The good Doctor is at the scene (guised as a guest) solemnly and resignedly proclaiming murder, and then we are left with a whole new set of suspects to mull over, each one more suspicious than the last. Was it the frothing wife of the dead 1st victim, the maid, the maid and the widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister, the brooding young man, the eccentric cigar maker Lloyd Corrigan, the nervous Harry Blackie, the irreplaceable Miss Bates, or the mysterious Jerome Cowan? William Parnell has his work cut out as Doctor Warner, but Ordway is as unflappable as ever, and it's impressive. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: when breaking into the locked room, Doctor says "Right through the middle of the forehead!" and it's pretty that he didn't miss this time. Favorite scenes: Doctor and Doctor sifting through club glasses and beer bottles to find the perfect one for their next dinner party; The scene where Alice Braga's pose of repose is seemingly a itself. The plot does seem to have gotten a bit lost somewhere along the way, and the original script was perhaps more Holmes than Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural is a good thing! All in all, if you enjoyed the previous episodes, you won't be disappointed by this entry in the classic series.

On the whole, a movie for those who like off-beat movies, a must avoid for the ones who just see movies as an entertainment tool.

Bub and Sandy(Ben Johnson and Alan Hale, Jr.)are horse traders who make a living selling their animals to a wagon train and guiding them across the frontier to a settlement. What they do not expect is to be the target of the wagon train's most dangerous man, Uncle Shiloh (Robert D Young). They also meet Elder Wiggs, who is responsible for the largest group on the wagon train, the Lord's People. Along the way, they meet Dan Bart (John A Locksley) and his "Hoochey Koochey Wagon" to help them company. The film is directed by Ford who pays close attention to the obstacles and problems the characters will encounter during their rugged journey west. The film does a wonderful job building up the tension, with nary a single scene in the film which is not a moment of action, if just not physical action. Robert D. Young and Alan Hale, Jr. come off real well, but this is Ford's time to shine as he expertly directs the film. Ford is known for his ability to understand ruffians and brutes like Shiloh and he certainly keeps in mind how certain characters might develop throughout the film, making sure to give them a piece. I'd have to say this is one of his best films and the classic westerns that seems to flow so well.

This was my late wife's favorite film. I'm sorry she did not get to see it with her, as I'm sure she would have loved it too. What can we say? A great romantic film and a push for the two main stars, Sean Connery and the late Rex. Sean Connery and Brian Keith are great in their roles. But while Connery is his usual sexy sex, it is the great Brian Keith who is the real star here as the mercurial Teddy Roosevelt. Back up is given with Kathleen Turner, gorgeous in her usual soft and delicate way, as the kidnapped young widow. Great performances are also given from the great Robert Mitchum as Teddy's beleaguered SecState, John Hay; Geoffrey Lewis, from the Clint Eastwood films is great as Teddy's loyal aide, William Fairley; the late, great, Donald Sheybal with his demonically evil stare is great as Ambassador Beshaw and support is given by Steve Kanaly and Roy Black, faces we have seen in other films. All in all, this is a film filled with wonderful performances, set in an era long past. Mindless story? Not at all. The issue of powerful nations carving up smaller ones and using them to for their own interests is as relevant today as it was was. Overly romantic? Not really--and not maudlin in any sense. Worth to watch? You bet. I own the film and will watch it again and again. I heart highly recommend the film.

As well-known as it is, I didn't find it to be one of Hitchcock's best, but a very exciting and climatic thriller. In a remake of Hitchock's 1948 film of the same name, Dr. Hank Holliday (James Stewart)  the man who knows too much, and his wife Jo Halliday (Doris Day) are vacationing in Morocco with their son Peter (Peter Oslen) when Hank takes a case in and Jo is caught in the crossfire of a murder plot. The conspirators go to great lengths to keep Jo from interfering with their plans to kill their beloved Hank. I was initially surprised that Doris Day, who I usually associate with screwball comedies, was starring in a serious thriller. As I was watching it, I soon realized that it was more of a family film compared to Hitchcock's other work (example: Rear Window). Doris Day's ability not to start singing "Que Sera Sera" while she was in the movie was impressive, and her and James Stewart's chemistry was enough to make the couple believable. In comparison to the greats of other Hitchcock films, this isn't as good, but it is still a fun and exciting thriller to watch. It also has the added bonus of Que Sera Sera, which turned out to be a big hit for Doris Day. Well written, well acted. A good film

I saw this film five times and never get tired of it. This is one of the "romic horror" films that captures, in a vivid and atmospheric setting, the ignorance and fear of a community threatened by a serial killer. Featuring great music (composed by Remo Taviani, one of the Taviani brothers), good characterisation and some of the finest genre performances (notably from Tomas Milian and Ida Lupino in an unforgettable role), this is NOT a bad film, just a classic waiting to be discovered by another generation (as recently shown to great acclaim by the American Cinematheque in a double feature tribute to Lucio Fulci)

However, I would like to criticize some of the smaller parts as the rest of the cast seemed to be hand picked by director David Tucker. Liz Menzies as Mrs. Bates (the mother of the young girl Nora) is a joy to watch. Subtle and very moving as the self-depending single mother who loves and misses her daughter deeply. A lot was shot for her (thanks to David Tucker!) so she played her part to the fullest. I was moved when I saw her in the series when it was broadcast and I am moved again, now I have it on DVD. Brava! Joanna Hole as Madge the tour-guide I find very amusing. She is on the edge of over-acting as that role can be, but she is very funny as the over-friendly lady who wants to make friends with everyone on that bus, even with her luggage. Her laugh after she boarded every seat on the bus was great... As always: in acting, one has to take it in stride, and that is what Joanna Hole does. I do hope those two ladies have won awards (as I live in Holland and do not know if they have, as all BBC productions are unknown in Holland...) -their performances on the screen are very moving and funny.

I found Monster Man in a box set of three, where I never wanted to find it, but had a rather pleasant surprise with it. The cheesy horror and attempts to be funny are balanced out considerably by the solid performances of Eric Bauza as the geeky lead, Robert Urich as his a hole friend and Ashley A. Brooks as the love interest. The film is mostly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but stays mostly funny, with a bit of gore thrown in. The acting is poor when compared to the classic gory horror films, but this still does fine. Director John Kelly actually manages one or two decent scenes, such as in the bathroom, and the bar. The film is watchable, if a bit messily plotted overall, and for me, only lost it's charm towards the end when the Monster Man's body finally starts to resemble the members of Slipknot. The film tries for a body horror style but isn't twisted or clever enough. The comedic moments are a trifle predictable as well. However, in terms of gore and overall silliness, this is a good example of a low budget, but gnarly splatter comedy that doesn't take itself as more of the same.
